questions.q: For the 3-node path graph with edges (0,1) and (1,2), what is the true maximum cut, and which assignments achieve it?
questions.explain: Putting node 1 alone in one group cuts both edges (0,1) and (1,2) simultaneously, giving a maximum cut of 2, achieved by (0,1,0) or its mirror (1,0,1).

questions.q: What approximation ratio did the best depth-1 QAOA simulation achieve on this 3-node path graph?
questions.explain: The best depth-1 expected cost found was ≈1.6495 out of a true optimum of 2, giving an approximation ratio of ≈0.8248 -- better than the 4-cycle's depth-1 ratio of ≈0.75 because this smaller graph is simpler for one layer to handle.

questions.q: In the tuned depth-1 probability table, what probability does the circuit assign to each of the two optimal bitstrings (0,1,0) and (1,0,1)?
questions.explain: Each of the two cost-2 (fully cut) bitstrings carries probability 0.3345, together accounting for 66.9% of all measurement outcomes -- far more than their 1-in-8 (0.125) share under a uniform distribution.

questions.q: What is the practical 'best-of-many-shots' readout strategy described in this lesson?
options: Run the circuit many times, keep a running tally, and report the best (highest-cut) bitstring actually measured, rather than trusting any single shot
Run the circuit exactly once and always trust that single measurement as the final answer
Average all measured bitstrings together into one fractional bitstring
Discard all measurements and only use the theoretical expected value
questions.explain: Because QAOA's output is a probability distribution, not a guaranteed single answer, practical use involves running many shots and reporting the best bitstring actually observed, while using the measured expectation value to keep improving the parameters.

questions.q: Compared to the uniform baseline probability of 0.125 for every basis state (before any cost or mixer unitary is applied), how did the tuned depth-1 circuit change the probabilities of the all-same-group states (0,0,0) and (1,1,1)?
options: It suppressed them sharply, down to about 0.0098 each, since they cut zero edges
It increased them to 0.3345 each, since they are the most common bitstrings
It left them unchanged at exactly 0.125 each
It eliminated all other bitstrings entirely, leaving only these two
questions.explain: The all-same-group bitstrings cut zero edges, and the tuned circuit suppresses their probability from the uniform 0.125 down to about 0.0098 each -- a concrete example of QAOA skewing probability away from bad solutions.
